title: Low-Rank Hierarchical Merging for Efficient Long-to-Short Reasoning
claim: Our method dominates the accuracy–length trade-off, and the sensitivity score we use pinpoints which components are critical to performance.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side: Pareto scatter left, degradation curves right with shaded gap
description: Two line and scatter plots sit side by side. The left panel plots average accuracy (y) against average response length in tokens (x). Merging methods appear as colored markers (squares, circles, stars, diamonds, triangles) in a legend-keyed palette: light blue for standard merging, mid blue for activation-guided, dark blue for ORCA, and red or orange for the proposed LHM variants. A red dashed Pareto frontier curves up and to the left, and the red LHM star sits at the top-left corner, labeled LHM-AIM. Baselines cluster lower and to the right, and Model Soup is farthest right. The right panel plots relative accuracy change (y) against merge coefficient reduction (x). A red solid line for high-LSOS layers drops steeply to about -34%. A blue dashed line for low-LSOS layers declines only gently. The area between the two lines is shaded peach. The eye goes first to the red star, then to the widening gap on the right.
caption: (Left) Accuracy–length Pareto plot across merging methods on the 1.5B benchmark suite. LHM (star) dominates all baselines by simultaneously achieving higher accuracy and shorter responses. (Right) Relative accuracy degradation when the merge coefficient is reduced by 0.2 for high-LSOS versus low-LSOS layers, confirming that second-order sensitivity identifies layers critical to reasoning performance.
abstract: Long-to-Short (L2S) model merging seeks to combine the strong reasoning capability of long chain-of-thought models with the concise style of base models, but existing methods that rely on linear interpolation and first-order activation statistics fail to capture how the loss landscape responds to parameter displacement, leading to degraded accuracy on hard tasks. We propose Low-Rank Hierarchical Merging (LHM), a training-free framework that replaces heuristic statistics with lightweight second-order curvature information. LHM consists of three components: (1) a low-rank Hessian approximation that efficiently estimates per-layer Hessian traces via Hutchinson's estimator on random inputs, eliminating the need for task-specific data; (2) a Layer Second-Order Sensitivity (LSOS) index that combines Hessian trace with task-vector norm to quantify per-layer fusion difficulty; and (3) a Dual-Constraint Coefficient Mapping (DCCM) that converts LSOS scores into layer-adaptive merge coefficients while jointly satisfying a fusion-error bound and a global length-reduction target. Experiments across six mathematical benchmarks on 1.5B and 7B models show that LHM outperforms state-of-the-art methods such as ACM-TIES and ORCA, achieving over 4\% accuracy gain and up to 93.1\% reduction in output length relative to the long-CoT model.
